methods.label: Dissect into 24 congruent triangles
methods.explanation:
The repeated rotations suggest finding one small piece whose area determines the whole polygon. Let \(O\) be the common center. Rotating the arrangement by \(30^\circ\) permutes the three sheets, since square orientations differing by \(90^\circ\) are identical. Reflection in a line through \(O\) and a square corner also preserves the arrangement, fixing that sheet and interchanging the other two.

Join \(O\) to every boundary vertex. Each boundary side joins an outward square corner to an inward intersection. The rotations carry the 12 outward corners to one another, and reflection through a corner ray exchanges its two neighboring boundary sides. Therefore the resulting 24 triangles are congruent. They fill the polygon without overlapping interiors: along any ray from \(O\), each square occupies an interval beginning at \(O\), so their union does too.

Choose the upper-right corner \(V\) of the unrotated square. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of its top side and \(P\) the inward boundary vertex on segment \(MV\). Then \(OM=MV=3\). Neighboring outward corner rays are \(30^\circ\) apart. Reflection in their halfway line exchanges their sheets and fixes the third, placing the intervening inward vertex on that line. Thus \(\angle VOP=15^\circ\). The square diagonal gives \(\angle MOV=45^\circ\), so
\[
\angle MOP=45^\circ-15^\circ=30^\circ.
\]
In right triangle \(OMP\), put \(MP=x>0\). The side opposite \(30^\circ\) is half the hypotenuse, so \(OP=2x\). The Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
3^2+x^2=(2x)^2,
\qquad x=\sqrt{3}.
\]
Consequently \(VP=3-\sqrt{3}\). Its baseline is the square's top side, whose perpendicular distance from \(O\) is 3, so
\[
[OVP]=\frac12\cdot3(3-\sqrt{3}).
\]
Multiplying by 24, the polygon's area is
\[
24[OVP]=108-36\sqrt{3}.
\]
Since 3 is prime and hence squarefree, \(a=108\), \(b=36\), and \(c=3\). Therefore \(a+b+c=147\), choice \(\boxed{E}\).
